title: Technical deep dive: OpenTelemetry + token-level metrics for runtime performance
summary: Deep dive on instrumenting Redwood runtime with OpenTelemetry for token-level metrics, traces, and dashboards. Covered KV cache and batching span design, quantization effects on latency, VPC/on-prem OTLP ingestion patterns, and next steps for a pilot and benchmark run.
topics: Instrumentation points: request, model, KV cache, batching
OTLP export options for private/VPC deployments
Dashboarding in Grafana / Prometheus vs OTLP
Impact of quantization on latency and metric interpretation
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-22 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Alex, Priya (Redwood); Jordan, Sofia, David (Acme)

[00:00:00] Alex Johnson: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Alex from Redwood, AE. Today Priya and I will walk through how we instrument runtime for token-level metrics with OpenTelemetry and some gotchas for private deployments.

[00:00:18] Jordan Lee: Thanks Alex. We're mostly interested in token-level latency and being able to split downstream why a request is slow — is it batching, KV cache miss, or model kernel slowdown.

[00:00:33] Priya Shah: perfect — that's the goal. we'll show span design: request -> routing -> model-inference -> kv-cache -> batching. note that sometimes the kv cache is reported as K-V cache or just cache in our telemetry; transcripts often flip it to k-v or kv.

[00:01:02] Sofia Martinez: quick question: for our VPC deployment, we need OTLP to go to an internal collector behind mTLS. how do you recommend setting that up?

[00:01:18] Priya Shah: two paths: 1) push from the Redwood private runtime to your OTLP collector endpoint over TLS + mTLS; 2) use a sidecar collector inside the customer's cluster that pulls from the runtime over localhost. for air-gapped installs we support file-based export as well. we'll share config snippets.

[00:01:47] David Chen: from a security perspective we also need to ensure no customer PII leaves logs/metrics. can we strip prompts or redact at the agent?

[00:02:04] Alex Johnson: yes, telemetry is configurable. token-level timing is numeric only, but if you want prompt hashes or truncated prompt ids we can hash on-host before emitting. we don't export raw prompt text by default in token metrics.

[00:02:28] Jordan Lee: awesome. show us how a trace looks?

[00:02:36] Priya Shah: sure — slide 7 in the deck (link shared) shows a sample trace. span tree: root request span (route_id, customer_id), then routing span (model variant selection), then inference span which itself spawns per-batch spans, and sub-spans for kv-cache lookup, kv-cache miss fallback, kernel execution. the per-token timing is recorded as attributes and sometimes as child spans for heavy detail. note: per-token child spans can blow up trace size so we usually emit aggregations for production.

[00:03:15] Speaker 1: i saw in that doc you sometimes call it "kv cache" and sometimes "KV-cache" which confuses our mapping rules in grafana. can the naming be stable?

[00:03:29] Priya Shah: good call — we have naming conventions in our config repo. we'll send the canonical OTEL resource / span names. in practice teams map both.

[00:03:46] Jordan Lee: what's the overhead of token-level tracing? if we enable token-level metrics how much extra latency or CPU?

[00:03:58] Priya Shah: depends. light-weight timers as attributes are low overhead (~1–3% CPU and a few ms per request). if you emit one span per token the overhead and backend cost skyrockets. we recommend: token-level attributes + per-batch histograms exported at 1s interval, and sampling for full token-span traces for a small percent of calls.

[00:04:32] Alex Johnson: plus when you enable high-cardinality labels like prompt_id or user_id you get metric cardinality explosion. keep label sets small — use hashed ids and sample them.

[00:04:49] Sofia Martinez: on dashboards, we're on Grafana with Prometheus remote_write. we also use Honeycomb for traces. what's the preferred exporter?

[00:05:00] Priya Shah: OTLP via collector can fan-out to Prometheus, Honeycomb, Datadog, etc. for token histograms Prometheus is fine but be careful: Prometheus histograms aggregate at scrape time and can lose per-request context. Honeycomb or a trace backend is better for per-request debug. we'll share recommended dashboards: latency breakdown by kv-cache hit/miss, batch size distribution, quantization profile.

[00:05:35] Jordan Lee: can you walk through an example of a KV cache miss?

[00:05:41] Priya Shah: yeah — example: request arrives -> routing picks gpt-like-variant -> batcher groups 4 requests -> before kernel we check kv-cache span: hit or miss attribute. on miss, we record kv-cache miss span and the fallback retrieval which costs extra 8–12 ms on our tests. the batch span will show increased tail latency. we annotate batch_size and kv_miss_count.

[00:06:12] Alex Johnson: shared benchmark from our lab: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/kv-cache.csv (placeholder) — in quantized models the kernel exec time decreased but deserializing quant tables added ~2ms per request in our setup.

[00:06:36] David Chen: about quantization — if we use int8 kernels, do metrics change semantics? can we still compare token latency across quantized and fp16 models?

[00:06:49] Priya Shah: you can compare but annotate model_variant and quantization_profile. quantized kernels reduce compute time but sometimes increase variance due to packing/unpacking. include those labels in traces. and we recommend separate dashboards for quantized vs reference.

[00:07:10] Speaker 1: do you expose KV hit rate as a time-series? we'd like to alert on when hit rate drops below 85%.

[00:07:18] Priya Shah: yes, we emit kv_cache_hit_rate as a gauge. we also emit per-route kv_cache_miss_count and per-second eviction metrics. alerting on a rolling window is best.

[00:07:32] Jordan Lee: sampling strategy — how to keep storage costs down but still get good signal?

[00:07:38] Priya Shah: recommended: 0.1% full token-span sampling for traces, 100% token timing attributes but aggregated per-batch histograms emitted at 1s; and dynamic sampling that increases sampling rate on error or latency spike.

[00:07:56] Alex Johnson: also important is correlating traces with logs and request ids. propagate a redwood_request_id in headers so you can jump from trace to full request logs.

[00:08:10] Sofia Martinez: our security team wants to host OTLP collector inside our VPC and only accept data from whitelisted IPs. is that supported?

[00:08:19] Priya Shah: yes — private deployment supports network ACLs, static egress IPs, and we can negotiate mTLS cert rotation with your PKI. we'll send our recommended cert rotation runbook.

[00:08:37] Jordan Lee: any gotchas when using the Redwood Dedicated vs Private runtime?

[00:08:44] Priya Shah: Dedicated (hosted dedicated capacity) can push metrics to Redwood-managed observability if you want us to host dashboards. Private -> everything stays in your network; you control collector endpoints and retention. Dedicated gives an easier onramp but Private gives total control for compliance.

[00:09:05] Speaker 1: how about disk-based KV cache metrics for on-prem? we have intermittent network so we prefer local cache stats.

[00:09:13] Priya Shah: runtime emits local cache stats to the collector; for air-gapped we also support periodic dumps to s3/on-prem object storage that you can ingest. file-based exporter is in the docs.

[00:09:32] Jordan Lee: can you share the OTEL config?

[00:09:36] Alex Johnson: yes — link: https://redwood.ai/docs/otel-config (placeholder). the snippet shows resource attributes, span names, metric instruments, and an example collector pipeline. we'll send the snippet after the call.

[00:09:49] Priya Shah: also a note on instrumentation: avoid high-cardinality attributes (full user_id, full prompt text). use hashed_user_id and prompt_hash. store a separate mapping offline if you need to join.

[00:10:06] Jordan Lee: what about retention — we have strict audit requirements for 13 months. can you configure retention on the export side?

[00:10:14] Priya Shah: retention is controlled by your backend (e.g., Prometheus long-term storage or Honeycomb retention policies). we can route to S3 bucket for long-term raw trace storage if needed. Redwood's private add-on can also store immutable audit logs for 13+ months.

[00:10:32] David Chen: do you provide a pre-built Grafana dashboard?

[00:10:36] Priya Shah: yes — we'll share a dashboard JSON (Grafana) with panels: token latency p50/p90/p99, kv_cache_hit_rate, batch_size distribution, per-model variant latency, quantization impact. link in artifacts.

[00:10:54] Alex Johnson: let's demo a short run — Priya, can you pull up an example trace?

[00:10:58] Priya Shah: sure — loading a Honeycomb trace (simulated).

[00:11:10] Priya Shah: here we see request id R-123 -> batch span (size=4) -> kv-cache miss for one request -> kernel exec and tail latency spike. attributes: batch_size=4, kv_miss_count=1, model_variant=redwood-llama-quant-int8.

[00:11:39] Jordan Lee: that match what we saw in our logs. interesting that kv miss added ~9ms.

[00:11:45] Sofia Martinez: regarding alerting, do you emit percentiles or do we compute them in the backend?

[00:11:52] Priya Shah: we emit histograms which backends can convert to percentiles; some backends compute approximations client-side. for high-resolution percentiles use a trace-based approach or a dedicated histogram exporter.

[00:12:11] Jordan Lee: ok next steps — we'd like a pilot with sample traffic and explicit SLOs: 99th percentile tail < 120ms for our chat endpoints.

[00:12:22] Alex Johnson: perfect. we'll run a small benchmark on a dedicated nodepool in our lab, then run a pilot in your staging VPC if you're comfortable. we'll need: sample payloads, expected concurrency, and SLOs.

[00:12:35] David Chen: security needs: SOC2 artifact, cert rotation doc, and mTLS config.

[00:12:42] Alex Johnson: we'll include SOC2 summary and the cert rotation runbook.

[00:12:48] Priya Shah: also we'll provide an OTEL collector config and Grafana dashboard JSON. for the pilot we'll enable token timing attributes + 0.5% full-token-span sampling.

[00:13:00] Speaker 1: small note — transcription sometimes changes Redwood product names; we saw "Redwood Dedicated" mis-typed as "Redwood Dedicate" in some docs. not a blocker.

[00:13:10] Alex Johnson: haha, thanks for flagging.

[00:13:15] Alex Johnson: recap and next steps — we'll: 1) send OTEL config snippet and Grafana JSON; 2) share benchmark CSV and sample run results; 3) schedule pilot run in staging for next week; 4) provide security docs (SOC2 + cert rotation).

[00:13:34] Jordan Lee: sounds good. can you send a timeline?

[00:13:37] Alex Johnson: yes, tentative timeline in notes: OTEL config and dashboards by 2026-07-24, sample benchmark results by 2026-07-26, pilot kickoff 2026-07-28.

[00:13:52] Priya Shah: action items we'll capture below.

[00:14:00] Alex Johnson: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the pilot.

[00:14:10] meeting ended

Share benchmark CSV and lab results by 2026-07-26
Schedule pilot kickoff in Acme staging for 2026-07-28
